editorial.hook: Elephants have a surprising social life
canva_fact_lines: African savanna elephants sometimes greet through trunk contact.
At a Thai camp, Asian elephants used reassuring touch after distress.
Young female African elephants can comfort and protect calves.
Wild African elephants use name-like calls for specific individuals.
In a rope task, Asian elephants waited for partners before pulling.
Captive Asian elephant females can bond with unrelated females.
African elephants can recognize family members through urine scent.
editorial.caption: From greeting and caring for calves to cooperation and recognizing family members, elephant societies are full of nuanced behavior. These examples come from published research; some observations were in captivity or controlled tasks. #Elephants #AnimalBehavior #Wildlife

candidate.claim_text: African savanna elephants sometimes greet one another through trunk contact.

candidates.canva_line: African savanna elephants sometimes greet through trunk contact.

sources.title: Function of Trunk-Mediated “Greeting” Behaviours between Male African Elephants: Insights from Choice of Partners
sources.supports: Reports trunk-to-mouth, temporal-gland and genital contact called greeting behaviours among male African savanna elephants; no claim that all contacts have only a greeting function.

candidates.semantic_caveat: The cited primary study observes males; the claim says sometimes, not all elephants or every encounter.

candidate.claim_text: Asian elephants at a Thai camp showed reassuring physical contact after another elephant became distressed.

candidates.canva_line: At a Thai camp, Asian elephants used reassuring touch after distress.

sources.title: Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) reassure others in distress
sources.supports: Field observations found more directed physical contact and vocal affiliation after distress than during control periods; the study notes possible common-stimulus confounding.

candidates.semantic_caveat: Camp setting and observed response are explicit; do not assert proven empathy or the distress trigger.

sources.title: African elephants address one another with individually specific name-like calls
sources.supports: Machine-learning analysis and playback experiments support individually specific receiver-directed calls; a 2025 correction changed values, not qualitative conclusions.

candidates.canva_line: In a rope task, Asian elephants waited for partners before pulling.

sources.title: Elephants know when they need a helping trunk in a cooperative task
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.supports: In cooperative two-end rope experiments, elephants delayed pulling until partners arrived, with task-specific access controls; behaviour may also be learned contingency.

candidates.semantic_caveat: Limited to experimental task; avoid claims of generalized human-style cooperation.
